knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# The card is not shipped with EMC2: every chunk that needs it is eval = FALSE, and
# what it printed is read from data/using-a-trained-flow.RData, written by
# system.file("scripts", "using_a_trained_flow_data.R", package = "EMC2").
load("data/using-a-trained-flow.RData")
show <- function(x) cat(sub("\n$", "", x), sep = "\n")

This vignette takes a neural likelihood trained outside *EMC2*, a *card*, and
fits data with it: register the card, check it, build a design and a prior
that respect it, fit one subject, and compare the fit with the analytic
likelihood on the same data. The card is `ddm_svst0_e299`, a normalizing flow
for *EMC2*'s `DDM` with drift-rate variability `sv` and non-decision-time
variability `st0` free. The card is not part of *EMC2*, so the code below is
not run when the vignette is built; what it printed comes from the script
`system.file("scripts", "using_a_trained_flow_data.R", package = "EMC2")`,
which regenerates every number here from the card in about half a minute on
six cores (`r ut$env$machine`, `r ut$env$R`).

## 1. The card

A card is one JSON file: the network's weights, its spline, the names of its
inputs and the scale each is given on, the region of parameter space it was
trained on (the *box*), the parameters it holds fixed, and golden vectors to
check it with. Cards are made by **nleflow**, a Python package that trains a
flow from a model specification and a simulator and exports the result
(`nleflow spec` -> `simulate` -> `train` -> `export`). Its `START_HERE.md`
(the NLE repository, `nleflow/START_HERE.md`; at the time of writing a
private repository, <https://github.com/andrewheathcote/nle>, branch
`nleflow-plan`) explains how to install it, and its `TUTORIAL.md` makes a
card in about half an hour. The format, the contract between nleflow and
*EMC2*, is `vignette("neural-likelihood-cards")`.

This card is `r ut$card_info$file` (sha256 `r substr(ut$card_info$sha256, 1, 16)`...),
kind `r ut$card_info$kind`: a spline flow over rt given the parameters and the
response, and a classifier for the probability of the second response. It was
trained for `r ut$card_info$training$epochs` epochs on 24 million simulated
trials (nleflow's `examples/ddm_svst0`).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
card <- "ddm_svst0_e299_weights.json"      # from the NLE repository, handover/nle-methods/port/export/
j <- jsonlite::fromJSON(card)
j$kind; j$context_names; j$fixed
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ut$card_info$kind; ut$card_info$context_names; as.list(ut$card_info$fixed)
```

Its inputs and the box (natural scale), with the transform each input is
given to the network on:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ut$card_info$box
```

`sv` and `st0` are *zero-box* inputs: the box includes exactly zero, and the
flow was trained on four regimes (both free, `sv = 0`, `st0 = 0`, both zero),
so the card gives the exact-zero models as well (`zerobox_c` is the
encoding's scale). `s` and `SZ` are not inputs: training held them at the
values in `fixed`, `s = 1` (the DDM's scale) and `SZ = 0` (no start-point
variability). Outside the box the network returns its floor, log density
`r round(ut$card_info$ll_floor_log, 1)`.

`register_nn_model()` turns the card into an *EMC2* model. `twin = DDM` names
the analytic model the card approximates; the registered model borrows its
parameter names, transforms, defaults and simulator, and replaces its
likelihood:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
m <- register_nn_model(card, twin = DDM)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show(ut$reg$messages)
```

Section 4 comes back to this message: the card says nothing about whether its
posteriors are calibrated. The card's `fixed`
values become the model's exceptions, so `s` and `SZ` can only be held at 1
and 0 (an exception that contradicts `fixed` is refused):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
m()$nn$fixed
m()$p_types
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ut$reg$fixed
ut$reg$p_types
```

The first check is that *EMC2* computes what the exporter computed: the
golden vectors beside the card (`ddm_svst0_e299_golden.csv`) are the
exporter's log densities at 1150 points, which `nn_golden_check()` recomputes
with *EMC2*'s compiled evaluator:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
nn_golden_check(m)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show(ut$golden)
```

The same check, together with the cards that ship with *EMC2*, is one
command, which installs nothing and needs no R session of your own:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# in a shell:  Rscript -e 'source(system.file("scripts", "nle_verify.R", package = "EMC2"))' ddm_svst0_e299_weights.json
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show(ut$verify)
```

## 2. A design and a prior

The design is an ordinary `DDM` design with the registered model in place of
`DDM`: drift rate by stimulus, everything else one value. `s` and `SZ` are
constants at the card's `fixed` values, on the sampled scale (`s` is sampled
on the log scale, `SZ` on the probit scale):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
des <- design(factors = list(subjects = 1, S = c("left", "right")), Rlevels = c("left", "right"),
              formula = list(v ~ S, a ~ 1, t0 ~ 1, Z ~ 1, sv ~ 1, st0 ~ 1),
              constants = c(s = log(1), SZ = qnorm(0)), model = m)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show(ut$design_messages); show(ut$design_nn)
```

**The prior must stay inside the box.** Where a parameter vector leaves the
box the network returns its floor, which cuts the posterior off there.
`nn_in_box()` maps the prior's mean +- 4 sd of every parameter to the natural
scale, cell by cell of the design, and compares it with the box. A first try:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pmean <- c(v = 0, v_Sright = 1, a = log(1.2), t0 = log(.25), Z = 0, sv = log(.8), st0 = log(.1))
pri <- prior(des, type = "single", pmean = pmean,
             psd = c(v = 1, v_Sright = 1, a = .3, t0 = .2, Z = .2, sv = .3, st0 = .3))
nn_in_box(des, pri)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ut$box_wide
show(paste("Warning message:", ut$box_wide_warning, sep = "\n"))
```

The right-stimulus drift rate (`v + v_Sright`) and the boundary separation
`a` leave the box. Narrower sds on `v`, `v_Sright` and `a` keep the prior
inside:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pri <- prior(des, type = "single", pmean = pmean,
             psd = c(v = .6, v_Sright = .6, a = .15, t0 = .2, Z = .2, sv = .3, st0 = .3))
nn_in_box(des, pri)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ut$box_ok
```

`nn_cell()` and `run_sbc()` refuse a prior that fails this check; a fit does
not, so check before fitting.

**The rt resolution.** `make_emc()` floors response times to its
`rt_resolution`, by default 1/60 s (a 60 Hz screen). When `t0` is sampled, that
moves every rt earlier by up to 16.7 ms, and `t0`, which is bounded by the
fastest responses, follows: in the NLE project's simulations the default
biased `t0` by about -1.9 posterior sds at 100 trials, for the analytic
likelihood as much as for a network. `make_emc()` warns when a
neural-likelihood design is given a coarse resolution:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
emc <- make_emc(dat, des, prior_list = pri)      # the default rt_resolution = 1/60
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
show(paste("Warning message:", ut$coarse_warning, sep = "\n"))
```

so give it the resolution the data were recorded at, 1 ms or finer:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
emc <- make_emc(dat, des, prior_list = pri, rt_resolution = 1/1000)
```

## 3. One subject, fitted with the card and with the analytic DDM

One subject, `r ut$data_summary$n` trials (200 per stimulus), simulated from
the analytic `DDM` (not from the network) at values inside the box, with
`sv` and `st0` above zero (on the natural scale, `v` = -1 for the left
stimulus and 1 for the right, `a` = 1.3, `t0` = 0.3 s, `Z` = 0.45, `sv` = 1,
`st0` = 0.15 s). The same data, design (with `DDM` as the model), prior and
seed are then fitted with the analytic likelihood. The chains run in
parallel, in forked processes, so the seed fixes the fit only with R's
`"L'Ecuyer-CMRG"` generator. Three chains of two cores each use six cores.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
des_ddm <- design(factors = list(subjects = 1, S = c("left", "right")), Rlevels = c("left", "right"),
                  formula = list(v ~ S, a ~ 1, t0 ~ 1, Z ~ 1, sv ~ 1, st0 ~ 1),
                  constants = c(s = log(1), SZ = qnorm(0)), model = DDM)
pri_ddm <- prior(des_ddm, type = "single", pmean = pmean,
                 psd = c(v = .6, v_Sright = .6, a = .15, t0 = .2, Z = .2, sv = .3, st0 = .3))
truth <- c(v = -1, v_Sright = 2, a = log(1.3), t0 = log(.3), Z = qnorm(.45), sv = log(1), st0 = log(.15))
set.seed(20261020)
dat <- make_data(truth, des_ddm, n_trials = 200)

emc_card <- make_emc(dat, des, prior_list = pri, rt_resolution = 1/1000)
set.seed(1)
emc_card <- fit(emc_card, cores_per_chain = 2, cores_for_chains = 3)

emc_ddm <- make_emc(dat, des_ddm, prior_list = pri_ddm, rt_resolution = 1/1000)
set.seed(1)
emc_ddm <- fit(emc_ddm, cores_per_chain = 2, cores_for_chains = 3)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ut$data_summary$table
```

Posterior means and 95 % intervals on the sampled scale (log for `a`, `t0`,
`sv`, `st0`; probit for `Z`), from `get_pars(emc, selection = "alpha")`.
`shift` is the card's posterior mean minus the analytic one, in analytic
posterior sds; `sd ratio` is the ratio of the posterior sds; `overlap` is the
part of the analytic interval that the card's interval covers.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
cmp <- ut$comparison
tab <- data.frame(parameter = cmp$parameter, true = round(cmp$true, 3),
                  card = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", cmp$card_mean, cmp$card_lower, cmp$card_upper),
                  analytic = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", cmp$analytic_mean, cmp$analytic_lower, cmp$analytic_upper),
                  shift = sprintf("%+.3f", cmp$shift_sd), `sd ratio` = sprintf("%.3f", cmp$sd_ratio),
                  overlap = sprintf("%.2f", cmp$overlap), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab)
fs <- ut$fits
knitr::kable(data.frame(fit = c("card", "analytic DDM"),
                        seconds = round(c(fs$card$seconds, fs$analytic$seconds), 1),
                        `samples` = c(sum(fs$card$iter), sum(fs$analytic$iter)),
                        `max gd` = round(c(fs$card$gd_max, fs$analytic$gd_max), 3),
                        `min ESS` = round(c(fs$card$ess_min, fs$analytic$ess_min)),
                        check.names = FALSE))
```

The two posteriors agree: the means differ by at most
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(cmp$shift_sd)))` posterior sds, the sds by at most
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(abs(cmp$sd_ratio - 1)))` %, and the intervals
overlap by `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(cmp$overlap))` % or more. With
`r round(min(fs$card$ess_min, fs$analytic$ess_min))` or more effective
samples per fit the Monte Carlo error of each mean is about 0.03 posterior
sd, so differences of this size are mostly sampling noise. The card's fit
took `r round(fs$card$seconds, 1)` s and the analytic fit
`r round(fs$analytic$seconds, 1)` s, `r sprintf("%.1f", fs$analytic$seconds / fs$card$seconds)`
times longer; the analytic DDM with `st0 > 0` integrates over the
non-decision time, the network does not.

Both posteriors miss the true values by about the same amounts (`v_Sright`,
for example, is 1.78 and 1.76 against 2): that is this data set, not the
likelihood. `sv` is the least informed parameter, with the widest interval.

## 4. What the checks showed, and what they did not

The checks in section 1, and the gates nleflow ran when it exported the card
(its `examples/ddm_svst0/README.md`), test **the network and its transport**:
the card computes in *EMC2* what it computed in training (the golden check,
7.6e-12), the compiled and R paths agree, and the network is close to the
analytic DDM point by point (on 100 000 held-out simulated trials, 99 % within
0.1 log units, worst in the far tail beyond 3 s). The fit in section 3 shows
the two likelihoods give the same posterior on one data set.

None of this shows that the card's **posteriors are calibrated**. Point
accuracy is not calibration: a network's error that varies with the
parameters moves the posterior, and a small error repeated over hundreds of
trials, all in one direction, can move it by a sizeable part of a posterior
sd, which one data set will not reveal. That is checked over many data sets
simulated from the prior, against the analytic likelihood on the same data,
with the tools of `vignette("neural-likelihoods")`:

- `nn_cell()` builds a cell: one design and prior, twice, with the network
  and with its analytic control;
- `nn_score_bias()` (seconds) is the direction in which the network pulls
  the posterior, per trial; `nn_posterior_shift()` (about a minute) predicts
  an SBC cell's standardised bias without the sampler;
- `run_sbc()` (through `nn_sbc_cell()`, hours) is the confirmation:
  simulation-based calibration of the network and of its control.

For this card none has been run yet (its registration message says so);
until they have, use it as above, alongside the analytic likelihood, and
not in place of it.

## 5. The same card outside R

nleflow also writes a card as an ONNX graph, so that the same network can be
used without *EMC2* (for example by HSSM-style Python code, with nothing but
`onnxruntime`):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# in a shell, in nleflow/:
#   uv run nleflow onnx ddm_svst0_e299_weights.json                         # two graphs
#   uv run nleflow onnx-check ddm_svst0_e299_shared.onnx ddm_svst0_e299_weights.json
```

It writes two graphs, `trialwise` (a parameter vector per trial) and `shared`
(one parameter vector for a block of trials), both float64; each takes the
parameters on the card's stored scale, rt and the choice (-1 for the first
response, +1 for the second) and returns the log likelihood of each trial.
They match the golden vectors to about 3e-12. nleflow's `examples/onnx_use`
(`README.md` and `use_onnx.py`) uses the graphs with `numpy` and
`onnxruntime` only, and documents the conversion from natural parameters to
the stored scale.
